name: State of the Teutonic Order
summary: A crusader state on the Baltic, conquered from the pagan Prussians by German knights of the Teutonic Order; defeated by Poland–Lithuania at Grunwald (1410), it became the secular Duchy of Prussia in 1525.

knownFor.label: Malbork Castle
knownFor.note: Largest brick castle in the world.

location.value: Prussia and Livonia on the Baltic coast; the headquarters moved to Marienburg in 1309 and to Königsberg in 1466.

terrain.value: Low plains and forests along the Baltic, the Vistula delta, coastal lagoons, and the Masurian lake district.
terrain.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

climate.value: Cool and damp, with cold winters when rivers and lagoons froze and short summers for growing rye.
climate.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

resources.value: Grain (especially rye), Baltic amber from the Samland coast, timber, furs, wax and fish.
resources.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

disasters.value: The Black Death reached Prussia around 1349–50, followed by later plague outbreaks and floods in the Vistula delta.
disasters.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

population.value: About 220,000 inhabitants at the beginning of the 14th century; the page gives no peak figure.
population.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order (checked 13 Nov 2026)

urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

disease.value: Repeated plague outbreaks after 1349, plus epidemics in towns and during sieges.
disease.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

migration.value: German settlers from the Holy Roman Empire moved into Prussia in the 1200s–1300s, founding towns and villages under Kulm law.
migration.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

economicBase.value: Control of port cities and trade, especially with the Hanseatic League, plus shipbuilding and a Baltic naval presence. Grain and amber are not mentioned in the part of the page read.

tradeRoutes.value: Baltic and Hanseatic trade from Danzig, Elbing and Königsberg to Flanders and England; the Order itself was a Hanse member.
tradeRoutes.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

wealth.value: The Order became very rich around 1400 from estates, the amber monopoly and its own trading officials.
wealth.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

moneyAndTax.value: The Order minted silver schillings, counted in Prussian marks; it drew income from estates, tolls and the amber monopoly.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

inequality.value: Knight-brothers and German burghers above free farmers; many native Prussian peasants had fewer rights.
inequality.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

governmentType.value: A religious military order under a Grand Master (Hochmeister), elected by the General Chapter until 1525 and in practice only “first among equals”.

keyRulers.value: Hermann von Salza was Grand Master 1209–1239; Winrich von Kniprode (1351–1382) brought it to its height of prestige; Albert of Brandenburg, after converting to Lutheranism, secularised the Prussian lands in 1525.

succession.value: Grand Masters were elected for life by the Order’s chapter; the knights were monks with no heirs.
succession.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

institutions.value: The Grand Master, the General Chapter, and commanders (komturs) running districts from castles, plus town councils.
institutions.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

stability.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

eliteConflict.value: Towns and landed knights against the Order; they formed the Prussian Confederation in 1440 and rebelled in 1454.
eliteConflict.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

armyAndTech.value: Armoured knight-brothers, local levies, paid soldiers and western crusader guests; strong brick castles and early cannon by about 1400.
armyAndTech.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

majorWars.value: Battle of Grunwald, 15 July 1410, a Polish–Lithuanian victory that the page says marked the start of the state’s decline; Thirteen Years’ War 1454–1466, after the Prussian Confederation asked Casimir IV for support (he signed incorporation on 6 March 1454).
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order (checked 13 Nov 2026)

territoryChange.value: Second Peace of Thorn (1466): lost Danzig, Marienburg and western Prussia to Poland and became a Polish vassal.
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

alliancesRivals.value: Enemy of Poland and Lithuania, especially after their union in 1386; allied with Hanseatic towns and helped by western crusaders.
alliancesRivals.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; the Order was noted for efficient record-keeping and castle building.
inventions.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

scienceEducation.value: Cathedral, parish and town schools taught Latin; a university at Kulm was approved in 1386 but never opened.
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

openness.value: Open to trade and settlers from the west, but hostile to pagan and Orthodox neighbours.
openness.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

communicationTransport.value: Baltic shipping, the Vistula, Nogat and Pregel rivers, coastal lagoons, and roads between castles.
communicationTransport.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

religion.value: A Catholic religious order; many Prussians stayed pagan for a time; Albert of Brandenburg converted to Lutheranism before secularising the order’s Prussian lands in 1525.

languageWriting.value: German in daily use and government, Latin in the Church; Old Prussian declined but survived among peasants.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

artsArchitecture.value: Brick Gothic architecture, above all the great castle of Marienburg (Malbork), the Order’s headquarters from 1309.
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

socialStructure.value: Knight-brothers, German burghers, Prussian and German peasants.
socialStructure.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the Order, the Catholic faith and towns; native Prussians and German settlers slowly merged.
sharedIdentity.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

dailyLife.value: Most people lived in farming villages growing rye, wheat and barley, and kept cattle and pigs.
dailyLife.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

neighbours.value: Poland, Lithuania, Masovia, Pomerania and the Order’s Livonian branch to the north-east.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

ideasReligions.value: Crusading ideology justified war on pagans; at the Council of Constance (1414–18) Polish scholars attacked forced conversion.
ideasReligions.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

colonisation.value: Conquest of the pagan Baltic Prussians (1230–83), followed by German settlement of towns and villages.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

riseSignals.value: The Golden Bull of Rimini (March 1226) tied Prussia to the Order; the Knights began the Prussian Crusade in 1230. The 1224 decree of Frederick II placed the region under imperial immediacy but is not described as the founding.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order (checked 13 Nov 2026)

peakPeriod.value: At its greatest extent in the early 15th century the state included Chełmno Land, Courland, Gotland, Livonia, Estonia, Neumark, Pomerelia, Prussia and Samogitia; the page gives no total area. Marienburg was capital 1308–1454 (infobox), then Königsberg 1454–1525.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order (checked 13 Nov 2026)

declineSignals.value: Defeat at Grunwald (Tannenberg) by Poland–Lithuania in 1410, followed by heavy war costs and taxes.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

outcome.value: Second Peace of Thorn, 19 October 1466: the west became Royal Prussia and the rest a Polish fief. Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach resigned as Grand Master, adopted Lutheranism and became Duke of Prussia (Prussian Homage, 10 April 1525).
outcome.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order (checked 13 Nov 2026)

sources.value: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order.
sources.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles; population figures are estimates.
overallCertainty.source: Wikipedia: State of the Teutonic Order
